A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same OV-MER task, OV-MERD dataset, metrics, and CLUE-based benchmarks. Their text, equations, tables, figures, and appendices support reliable comparison despite extensive reorganization.

before.justification: v1 reports original benchmark, model-fusion, annotation, and metric-comparison results in Section 5 and the appendices.

after.justification: v2 retains original benchmark results and adds a label-informativeness user study and description-length correlation analysis.

M1.justification: The human-LLM annotation pipeline, CLUE variants, S2 generation procedure, and grouping methods remain unchanged. Expanded explanations of frame sampling, clue merging, and label retention document existing procedures rather than establish algorithm changes.

E1.justification: Section 5 adds a human judgment task comparing basic and OV labels for informativeness on existing OV-MERD samples. The underlying MER2023-derived video coverage and Chinese/English recognition evaluations remain. Additional datasets in the expanded comparison table are literature comparisons, not new evaluation datasets.

E2.justification: Table 2 retains the same comparators. However, v1 Table 3's six combinations of SECap or SALMONN with mPLUG-Owl, Video-ChatGPT, or Chat-UniVi disappear from v2, removing an auxiliary comparison branch.

E3.justification: The new informativeness study specifies four annotators, randomly selected samples, and binary judgments, but omits the sample count. Existing benchmark settings remain. Section 2 changes source-sampling wording from even to random selection, while the Ethics Statement retains even selection; actual resampling is not established.

E4.justification: v2 adds human informativeness evaluation, two annotator-specific case studies, description-length versus label-count correlations, and a numerical BLEU illustration in Section 5 and Appendices K, R, and T. It removes the model-fusion analysis. Existing strategy ablations and full emotion-wheel comparisons are retained, including relocated material.

E5.justification: Both versions specify two runs with means and standard deviations for benchmark experiments. Matched tables retain this reporting practice. The new analyses introduce no changed seed information, repeated-run policy, confidence intervals, or significance testing; Pearson correlation was already used in v1.

E6.justification: v2 newly reports 97.5% informativeness preference and length-label correlations of 0.3416 and 0.2939, and revises the reported emotion-category count from 248 to 236 without explaining why. Fusion results disappear, including SALMONN plus mPLUG-Owl's English Fs of 58.70±0.04. Table 2 and retained ablation and metric-comparison scores remain unchanged.

T1.justification: The emotion-wheel mappings, set-based precision, recall, F-score, and Jaccard definitions remain mathematically unchanged. Reformatted equations and the explicit statement of label-order invariance explain existing mathematics; no new formal derivation or proof is introduced.

C1.justification: The central task, dataset, metric, and benchmark contributions remain. v2 adds an Introduction contribution claiming experimentally demonstrated improvements in emotion representation and user experience. Its abstract also explicitly acknowledges that constructing a dataset covering the full emotional spectrum is infeasible.

C2.justification: v2 adds a Chinese-data and Chinese-annotator cultural limitation, discusses unresolved fusion ambiguities and fast-motion limitations, and qualifies the relationship between description length and label richness. Section 5 also identifies manually checked baselines as upper bounds and gives a dataset-specific explanation for weak text-only performance.

D1.justification: v2 explicitly documents zero-shot inference without training, identifies some annotators as team members, clarifies label acceptance across annotation rounds, and directs readers to MER2023 for raw data. It removes v1's statement that code and intermediate results are provided in supplementary materials. Prompts, model links, and hardware remain.

R1.justification: New Appendix A substantially positions OV-MER against one-hot, multi-label, partial-label, and fine-grained recognition, including their different solutions and label-space requirements. Added references cover these distinctions and additional datasets. Appendix G also introduces an explicit first-dataset claim for human-LLM collaborative annotation.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, and substantial introductory passages are rewritten. The former Discussion is redistributed into limitations and motivation appendices, and the appendix structure is extensively reordered and expanded with task comparison, construction rationale, and interpretation sections.

P2.justification: v2 revises Figure 1, restyles Figure 5, exchanges examples between the introduction and appendix, and adds duration and annotator-case figures. The fusion table is removed, while the full emotion-wheel table moves to Appendix S with a condensed version in the main text. These substantially change display organization.

improvement.justification: v2 improves task positioning, explains annotation decisions more clearly, states cultural limits, and adds targeted evidence about label informativeness and richness while retaining the main benchmark. The gain is limited: the user study omits its sample count and does not directly establish improved user experience, the category-count revision is unexplained, and useful fusion results and explicit code-availability information are removed.
